clinicalPearls: A progeroid form of autosomal recessive cutis laxa with a prematurely aged, wizened appearance from birth
Combines lax, thin, wrinkled skin with corneal clouding or cataract, intrauterine and postnatal growth restriction, and a large-appearing forehead
Neurological features are prominent: developmental delay, hypotonia, movement disorder (often athetoid) and sometimes hyperreflexia
Caused by variants in genes of the proline/glutamate biosynthesis pathway, chiefly ALDH18A1 and PYCR1, linking it to the wider cutis laxa spectrum
The face may show a triangular shape with a prominent forehead and sparse subcutaneous fat contributing to the aged look
Joint laxity and dislocations may occur alongside the skin findings
Management is supportive, addressing feeding, growth, developmental needs and the ophthalmic abnormalities
reference.pathophysiology: De Barsy syndrome is a progeroid cutis laxa caused by biallelic variants in ALDH18A1 or PYCR1, enzymes of the mitochondrial pathway that synthesises proline and ornithine from glutamate. Disruption of this pathway impairs collagen and elastin synthesis and mitochondrial function, weakening dermal connective tissue to produce lax, aged-looking skin and contributing to the neurological, ocular and growth abnormalities. The combined connective tissue and metabolic effects explain the striking progeroid appearance alongside the movement disorder and developmental delay.
additionalDifferentials: Other autosomal recessive cutis laxa types
Cockayne syndrome and other progeroid disorders
additionalInvestigations: Molecular testing of ALDH18A1 and PYCR1, usually via a cutis laxa gene panel
Ophthalmic examination for corneal clouding and cataract
Developmental and neurological assessment including for movement disorder
Skin examination and dermal histology for elastic fibre abnormalities where needed
Plasma amino acid studies where a metabolic contribution is investigated
redFlags: Failure to thrive with significant feeding difficulty
Progressive neurological deterioration or intractable movement disorder
Visual impairment from cataract or corneal clouding
Complications of severe hypotonia such as recurrent aspiration
reference.prognosis: The outlook is variable and often guarded, with significant developmental impairment and growth failure; some children have a shortened lifespan while milder cases survive longer with supportive care.
pitfalls: Confusing it with other progeroid or cutis laxa syndromes without molecular confirmation
Overlooking the movement disorder and attributing hypotonia to a non-specific cause
Missing the ophthalmic abnormalities that need early assessment
Assuming a uniformly poor prognosis when expressivity varies considerably
references: GeneReviews: ALDH18A1- and PYCR1-Related Cutis Laxa
Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Manage supportively through clinical genetics and paediatrics, as there is no disease-modifying therapy
Refer for ophthalmic assessment and treat corneal clouding and cataract surgically where indicated
Provide neurodevelopmental support with physiotherapy and occupational therapy for hypotonia, movement disorder and developmental delay
Monitor growth and give feeding and nutritional support for intrauterine and postnatal growth restriction
Protect the fragile, lax skin and manage joint laxity and dislocations with physiotherapy and orthopaedic input
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder (ALDH18A1, PYCR1), with carrier and reproductive counselling for the family
